title: Sun, Moon and stars: what lights and warms our sky

summary.text: Hold your hand in a patch of sunshine, and it soon feels warm. The Sun gives us light and heat, even though it is very far away. At night the Sun's light is gone from our sky, and we can see the Moon and the stars. The Moon makes no light of its own: it shines because the Sun lights it up. The stars are there in the daytime too. In a torch test, your child finds out why we cannot see them by day.
summary.art: A sky split in two: on the left a bright blue day sky with the Sun and a girl warming her hands at a window, on the right a dark night sky with a half Moon and many small stars over a block of flats.

intro.hook: Hold your hand in a patch of sunshine for a slow count of twenty. Now hold it in the shade. What do you feel?
intro.text: In the sunshine your hand gets warm. In the shade it stays cooler. The Sun is very, very far away, but its light still reaches your hand and warms it. At night that sunlight is gone from our sky, and the Moon and the stars show up. But where are the stars in the daytime? In this unit you find out.
intro.art: A child's hand held in a bright patch of sunlight on a tiled floor by a window, and the same hand in the shade next to it.
intro.parent: If no sunlight comes into your home, stand at a window or on a balcony in the day and let your child feel the sunlit glass or railing, and then a shaded part. Never let your child look straight at the Sun.

outcomes: By the end I can say that the Sun gives us light and heat.
By the end I can show that things in sunshine get warmer than things in the shade.
By the end I can say that the Moon makes no light of its own: the Sun lights it up.
By the end I can say that the stars are in the sky in the daytime too, and that the bright day sky hides them.
By the end I know I must never look straight at the Sun.

terms.meaning: The Sun is a star. It is a huge ball of very hot gas that gives us light and heat.
terms.example: Sunlight on a balcony railing makes the steel warm to touch.
terms.art: A big yellow Sun with short rays, and a small balcony railing below it with a hand touching it.

terms.meaning: A star is a huge ball of very hot gas that makes its own light. The stars at night are so far away that they look like tiny dots.
terms.example: On a clear night you can see a few bright stars from a balcony, even in a city.
terms.art: A dark sky with a few tiny white star dots over the roofs of some buildings.

terms.meaning: The Moon is a big round ball of rock that goes round the Earth. It makes no light of its own. It shines because sunlight falls on it.
terms.example: On a full Moon night, the Moon looks like a bright round plate.
terms.art: A grey round Moon with craters, lit brightly on one side by sunlight coming from a Sun at the edge of the picture.

terms.meaning: Shade is a place where sunlight is blocked, so it is cooler and less bright.
terms.example: On a hot day, people wait for the bus in the shade of a tree.
terms.art: A big neem tree throwing a dark patch of shade on the ground, with a woman and a girl standing in it out of the hot sunshine.

explanations.concept: The Sun gives light and heat
explanations.context: This card is about what the Sun gives us.
explanations.definition: The Sun is a star. It gives out light and heat all the time. When its light falls on something, that thing gets warmer.
explanations.description: In the ice test, the ice cube in the sunshine melted much faster than the one in the shade. The sunshine brought heat to it. The Sun is about 150 million kilometres away. That is so far that a car would take more than a hundred years to drive there. Its light still reaches us in about 8 minutes, and it warms everything it falls on: the floor, the water in a tank, your skin and the leaves of plants. Plants use sunlight to make their food, and humans and other animals eat plants.
examples: In the ice test, the ice cube in the sunshine melted first.
Clothes on a sunny balcony dry faster than clothes in the shade.
A crow sits in the morning sun with puffed-out feathers to get warm.
explanations.art: Two steel bowls on a floor: one in a sun patch with a small puddle and a tiny piece of ice, one in the shade with an ice cube still nearly whole.

explanations.concept: The Moon shines with the Sun's light
explanations.context: This card is about why the Moon looks bright.
explanations.definition: The Moon makes no light of its own. Sunlight falls on the Moon, and some of it bounces off and comes to our eyes.
explanations.description: The Moon looks bright at night, so many children think it makes light, like a lamp. It does not. The Moon is a ball of grey rock. The Sun shines on it, the way a torch shines on a steel plate. Some of that light bounces off the Moon and reaches us. That is why the Moon looks bright even when it is night where we are. We often see the Moon in the day too, as a pale white shape in the blue sky.
examples: A steel plate looks bright only when a lamp shines on it. The Moon looks bright only because the Sun shines on it.
On some mornings you can see a pale Moon in the blue sky.
In 2023, India's Chandrayaan-3 landed on the Moon and found grey rock and dust there.
explanations.art: The Sun on the left shining a beam of light onto a grey Moon, and the light bouncing from the Moon down to a girl on a balcony at night.

explanations.concept: The stars are in the sky in the daytime too
explanations.context: This card is about where the stars are in the day.
explanations.definition: The stars shine all the time, by day and by night. In the day, sunlight makes the whole sky so bright that we cannot see the stars' small light.
explanations.description: In the torch test, the little torch star was hard to see in the bright spot by the window. In the dark room, the same torch star shone brightly. The torch was the same both times. Only the light around it changed. The real stars work the same way. In the day, the Sun's light lights up the air, and the whole sky glows blue. The stars are still there, but their light is too faint to see in that bright sky. When the Sun sets and the sky goes dark, we can see them again.
examples: In the torch test, the star was hard to see by the sunny window and bright in the dark room.
During a total eclipse of the Sun, the Moon covers the Sun for a few minutes. The sky goes dark and bright stars appear in the middle of the day.
Big telescopes can find bright stars even in the daytime.
explanations.art: Two pictures of the same sky: a bright blue day sky with the stars drawn very faintly as dotted outlines, and the dark night sky with the same stars shining clearly.

explanations.concept: Why a city sky shows fewer stars
explanations.context: This card is about why you see more stars far from a city.
explanations.definition: Street lights, shop signs and lit windows light up the air over a city at night. Then only the brightest stars can be seen.
explanations.description: On a clear night in a big city, you may see only a few stars. In a village far from city lights, the sky can be full of thousands of them. The stars are the same. The city lights make the night air glow a little, the way the Sun makes the day sky glow a lot. The faint stars get hidden, and only the brightest ones show. Scientists call this light pollution: too much light at night, in places where it is not needed.
examples: From a city balcony you may count only five or ten stars.
Far from towns, in the Thar desert or the hills of Ladakh, the sky can be full of stars.
Switch off the lights near a window at night, and a few more stars show.
explanations.art: Two night skies side by side: over a city of bright tall buildings only three stars, and over a dark village with small huts a sky full of stars.

agreed.text: The Sun is a star. It gives the Earth light and heat.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can feel the Sun's warmth in a patch of sunshine. Scientists have measured the Sun's light from the ground and from spacecraft, such as India's Aditya-L1, which was launched in 2023 to study the Sun.

agreed.text: The Moon makes no light of its own. It shines with sunlight.
agreed.evidence: The Moon's lit side always faces the Sun. Spacecraft that landed on the Moon, such as India's Chandrayaan-3 in 2023, found grey rock and dust, not anything that glows.

agreed.text: The stars are in the sky in the daytime too.
agreed.evidence: During a total eclipse of the Sun, bright stars can be seen in the daytime sky. Big telescopes can see bright stars in the day.

challenging.claim: The Moon makes its own light, like a lamp.
challenging.who: A common idea among young children, and many grown-ups
challenging.for: The Moon is the brightest thing in the night sky, and it can light up a path at night.
challenging.against: The Moon is a ball of grey rock. Its bright side always faces the Sun. When the Moon goes into the Earth's shadow in an eclipse of the Moon, it goes dark red and dim, because sunlight cannot reach it.
challenging.context: This card is about the Moon's light.

challenging.claim: The stars go away in the daytime, and come out at night.
challenging.who: A common idea among young children
challenging.for: We see stars only at night. In the day the sky looks empty of them.
challenging.against: In the torch test, the torch star was still shining by the sunny window. It was only hard to see. During a total eclipse of the Sun, stars appear in the middle of the day, because the sky goes dark.
challenging.context: This card is about where the stars go in the day.

big_questions.q: In the torch test, the star was still shining by the sunny window, but you could hardly see it. What else might be there all the time that we cannot see?
big_questions.hint: Think of the stars in the day, the Moon on a cloudy night, or the air around you.

big_questions.q: The Moon has no light of its own, but it lights up the night. Is it right to call the Moon bright?
big_questions.hint: Think of a steel plate next to a lamp. Where does its brightness come from?

big_questions.q: The ice in the sunshine melted first. How did the heat get from the Sun, so far away, to the ice?
big_questions.hint: Nothing touched the ice except sunlight. The heat came with the light.

big_questions.q: Every star at night is a sun. Could a child far away, near another star, be looking at our Sun as a tiny dot tonight?
big_questions.hint: Our Sun is a star too. From very far away, it would look like a small dot.

story.title: Tara and the Hidden Stars
story.note: Ajji means grandmother in Kannada. Tara, Manu, Amma and Ajji are made up. Villages far from towns have much darker night skies than cities, so many more stars can be seen there.
text: Tara was six. She lived in a tall block of flats in Bengaluru, with her Amma and her little brother Manu.
From their balcony, Tara could see the Moon on many nights. But she could only ever count three or four stars. "Where are all the stars from my picture books?" she asked.
In the summer holidays, Amma took them on a long bus ride to a village in Karnataka. Their grandmother, Ajji, lived there in a small house with a flat roof.
The days in the village were hot and bright. Every morning, Ajji spread red chillies on a mat in the sunshine. "The Sun will dry them for us," she said.
Tara put her hand on the mat at noon. It was warm, almost hot. Then she put her hand on the floor inside the house, where no sunlight fell. It was cool.
"The sunshine warmed the mat," said Tara.
"Yes," said Ajji. "The Sun is very far away. But its light comes all the way here, and it brings heat with it."
That night, after dinner, Ajji took the children up onto the roof. She switched off the bulb by the stairs.
Tara looked up, and gasped. The sky was full of stars. There were big bright ones and tiny faint ones, more than she could ever count.
"Ajji!" said Tara. "The village has so many more stars than Bengaluru!"

Ajji smiled. "It is the same sky, Tara. The same stars are over Bengaluru tonight. But the city has so many lights that the night air glows. The faint stars get hidden. Here it is dark, so we can see them all."
Manu pointed at the Moon. It was a half Moon, high over the coconut trees. "Is the Moon a big lamp?" he asked.
"No," said Ajji. "The Moon makes no light of its own. The Sun shines on the Moon, the way a lamp shines on your steel tumbler. The Moon sends some of that sunlight down to us."
The next morning, Tara ran up to the roof. The sky was bright blue. There was not a single star.
"Ajji, where did the stars go?" she called.

Ajji came up with a small torch and a piece of cardboard. She fixed the cardboard over the front of the torch with a rubber band. She poked one tiny hole in it with a pencil point, and taped a bit of thin paper over the hole.
"This is our star," she said. She switched on the torch and stood in the bright sunshine, a few steps away. "Can you see it?"
Tara looked hard. She could only just see a dull little dot. Manu could not see it at all.
Then Ajji took them down into the dark storeroom, where the rice sacks were kept. She shut the door. The little torch star shone bright and clear.
"It was shining in the sunshine too!" said Tara slowly. "We just couldn't see it."
"That is right," said Ajji. "The real stars are like that. They shine all day. But the Sun lights up the whole sky, so it is too bright to see them."
"So the stars are up there right now?" asked Manu.
"Right now," said Ajji.
Back in Bengaluru, on the first night home, Tara stood on the balcony. She counted four stars. Then she switched off the balcony light and waited. She counted six.
"The others are there too," she told Manu. "They are just hidden."
story.epiphany: Tara finds that the stars never go away. The bright day sky hides them, and city lights hide the faint ones at night. On the way she also feels that sunshine brings heat, and learns from Ajji that the Moon shines only with the Sun's light.
ask: Why was the mat in the sunshine warm, and the floor inside cool?
Why could Tara see so many more stars from Ajji's roof?
Where does the Moon's light come from?
In the morning, where were the stars?
art: A grandmother spreading red chillies on a mat in bright sunshine on a flat roof, with a girl touching the warm mat.
A grandmother and two children lying on a flat roof at night, under a sky full of stars and a half Moon over coconut trees.
The grandmother holding a torch with a cardboard cap in bright sunshine, and the girl squinting to see a tiny dot of light.
The same torch shining a bright point of light in a dark storeroom with rice sacks, and the two children smiling.
A girl on a city balcony at night, her hand on the light switch, looking up at a few stars over tall buildings.

experiments.title: Where Do the Stars Go in the Day? The torch star test
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a tiny star from a torch and a piece of cardboard. Then you look at it in a bright place and in a dark room, to find out where the stars go in the daytime.
experiments.question: Does a small light still shine in a bright place? Can we see it there?
experiments.predict: We will look at the torch star by a bright window, and then in a dark room. Where will you see it best? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same torch, the same tiny hole and the same thin paper every time. You stand the same distance away, three big steps, every time. Only one thing changes: how bright it is around the star.
results_table: My guess: will I see it?
What I saw: bright, faint, or not at all

materials.item: a torch, or a phone with a torch
a piece of cardboard from an old box, a little bigger than the front of the torch
a rubber band or some tape
thin paper, such as notebook paper or tissue paper, 3 small squares
a bright place in the day: next to a sunny window, or on a balcony
a dark room, such as a bathroom with the door shut

experiments.safety: Never look at the Sun. Keep the Sun off to one side, out of your child's view.

schedule.what: Make a torch star, then look at it in a bright place and in a dark room.

experiments.record: Draw the torch star twice: once by the bright window, and once in the dark room. Draw it as big and bright as it looked each time.

setup.art: A grown-up fixing a piece of cardboard over the front of a torch with a rubber band, poking one tiny hole in it with a pencil, and taping a small square of thin paper over the hole.
setup.caption: 1. Cover the torch with cardboard. Make one tiny hole. Tape thin paper over it.

setup.art: The grown-up holding the switched-on torch next to a bright window in the day, and a girl three big steps away squinting at it, with the Sun not in view.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the star by a bright window.

setup.art: The same grown-up and girl in a dark bathroom, the tiny point of light from the torch shining clearly.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the same star in a dark room.

setup.art: In the dark bathroom, the girl switching the room light on, and the torch star becoming hard to see.
setup.caption: 4. Switch the room light on and off. Watch the star.

flow.do: Ask your child where the stars are in the daytime. Listen, and don't correct the answer.
flow.say: At night we can see stars in the sky. Where do you think the stars are in the daytime?
flow.kid: Where do the stars go in the day? What do you think?

ask.q: Where are the stars in the day?
good: They are on the other side of the sky.

flow.parent: Many children say the stars go away, go to sleep or switch off. Any answer is fine. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Put the cardboard over the front of the torch. 2. Hold it on with a rubber band or tape. 3. Poke one tiny hole in the middle with a sharp pencil point. 4. Tape one small square of thin paper over the hole. 5. Switch the torch on to check that only a dim dot of light comes out.
flow.say: We are making a pretend star. The torch light can only come out of this tiny hole, through a thin paper. That makes one small dim dot of light, like a star.
flow.kid: Watch the grown-up make the star. Light comes out of one tiny hole.
flow.parent: Push the pencil gently, with the torch lying on a table, away from fingers. The paper makes the dot dim, as real stars are. If the cardboard glows all over, use thicker cardboard or two layers.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess. Write or draw the guesses in the table.
flow.say: First we will hold the star by the bright window. Then we will take it into the dark bathroom. Where will you see it best? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Where will you see the star best? By the window, or in the dark? Why?

good: It is the same torch, so it will look the same.
It will look brighter in the dark.
In the sunshine it will get lost.

flow.parent: Wait for a guess and a reason. Do not say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Stand at the brightest window, or on the balcony, in the day. 2. Your child stands three big steps away, facing you. 3. Switch the star on and point it at your child. 4. Ask what they see.
flow.say: Here is our star, shining. Look at the hole in the cardboard. Can you see the star? Is it bright, faint, or can you not see it at all?
flow.kid: Look at the hole in the cardboard. Can you see the star?

good: I can only just see it.

flow.parent: Stand so the Sun is off to one side, not in your child's view. By a bright window, the dim star should look very faint or vanish. If your child still sees it clearly, tape on another square of paper and look again. Use that same star in the dark room. Let your child walk one step closer and back again.

flow.do: 1. Go into a dark room, such as a bathroom, and shut the door. 2. Switch off the light. 3. Stand three big steps apart again. 4. Switch the star on.
flow.say: Same torch, same hole, same three steps. Now we are in the dark. Can you see the star now? Is it bright or faint?
flow.kid: Same star, now in the dark. Can you see it? Bright or faint?

good: It looks like a real star.

flow.parent: In the dark, the same dim dot looks bright and sharp. This is the surprise. If you cannot see it in the dark either, take off one square of paper, then look again by the window with the same star. A little light under the door is fine.

flow.do: Keep the star shining. Switch the room light on, then off, then on again. Ask your child to watch the star each time.
flow.say: I am switching on the room light. Watch the star. Now I am switching it off. What happens to the star?
flow.kid: Watch the star. The room light goes on. Then off. What happens?

ask.q: Did the torch stop shining when the room light came on?
good: It was still shining, but hard to see.

flow.parent: The room light is like the Sun coming up. The star does not stop shining. The light around it makes it hard to see.

flow.do: Back in the bright room, look at the guesses. Ask your child what they think now, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Was the star shining by the window? Why was it hard to see there? So where do you think the real stars are in the daytime?
flow.kid: Was the star shining by the window? Where are the real stars in the day?

ask.q: Where are the real stars in the day?
good: They are there, but the sky is too bright to see them.

check.q: Nila, a girl in Class 1, holds the torch star by a sunny window. Her brother can hardly see it. Why?
options: The bright light around it hides the star
The torch stops shining in the day
check.why: The torch kept shining all the time. By the sunny window there was so much light around it that the small star was hard to see. The real stars are hidden in the day sky in the same way.

experiments.title: Sun or Shade: which ice cube melts first?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put one ice cube in the sunshine and one in the shade. You find out whether sunshine brings heat.
experiments.question: Does an ice cube melt faster in sunshine or in shade?
experiments.predict: One ice cube goes in the sunshine, one in the shade. Which will melt first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use two ice cubes of the same size, from the same tray. We use two bowls that are the same. We put them down at the same time, and we look at them at the same times.

materials.item: two ice cubes of the same size, from the same ice tray
two small steel bowls or katoris that are the same
a sunny spot: a patch of sunshine on the floor, a windowsill or a balcony
a shady spot in the same room or on the same balcony
a clock or a phone, to check the time

experiments.safety: Never look at the Sun. A sunny floor or railing can be hot, so touch it gently first.

schedule.what: Put one ice cube in the sunshine and one in the shade. Look at them every 5 minutes.

experiments.record: Draw the two bowls after 10 minutes. Show how big each ice cube was, and how much water was in each bowl.

setup.art: Two steel katoris side by side on a kitchen counter, each with one ice cube, and a girl holding them.
setup.caption: 1. Put one ice cube in each bowl.

setup.art: One katori in a bright patch of sunshine on the floor by a window, and the other in the shade a few steps away.
setup.caption: 2. One bowl in the sunshine, one in the shade.

setup.art: The girl and a grown-up looking into both bowls: the sunny one has a small piece of ice in a puddle, the shady one a bigger cube.
setup.caption: 3. Look every 5 minutes. Which melts first?

flow.do: Find a patch of sunshine and a shady spot nearby. Let your child touch the floor in both places.
flow.say: Put your hand on the floor in the sunshine. Now in the shade. Which feels warmer?
flow.kid: Touch the floor in the sun. Now in the shade. Which is warmer?
flow.parent: If no sunshine comes into your home, use a sunny windowsill or balcony. On a cloudy day, try again on a sunny one.

flow.do: Show the two ice cubes in their bowls. Ask your child to guess, and why.
flow.say: One ice cube will sit in the sunshine. One will sit in the shade. Which one will melt first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which ice cube will melt first? Why do you think so?

good: They will melt the same, because it is the same ice.

flow.do: Put one bowl in the sunshine and one in the shade, at the same time. Note the time.
flow.say: Ready? We put them down together. Now we wait five minutes.
flow.kid: Put them down together. Now we wait five minutes.

flow.do: Look at both bowls after 5 minutes and after 10 minutes. Each time, your child says which ice is smaller and which bowl has more water.
flow.say: Look into both bowls. Which ice cube is smaller? Which bowl has more water in it?
flow.kid: Look in both bowls. Which ice is smaller? Which has more water?

good: The ice in the sunshine is smaller.
The sunny bowl has more water.

flow.parent: In strong sunshine, the ice in the sun is clearly smaller after 5 to 10 minutes. In winter or weak sunshine, wait a little longer.

flow.do: Ask your child what they found and why.
flow.say: Which ice melted first? Nothing touched it except sunshine. So what did the sunshine bring?
flow.kid: Which ice melted first? What did the sunshine bring?

check.q: Revathi, a girl in Class 1, puts one ice cube in the sunshine and one in the shade. Which melts first?
check.why: Sunshine brings heat from the Sun. The ice in the sunshine gets more heat, so it melts first.

activities.title: What Is in the Sky Right Now? A window look
activities.context: In this activity you look out of a window in the day and say everything you can see in the sky. Then you guess what the night sky will show.

materials.item: nothing to buy: a window or a balcony, in the day

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun, not even for a moment, and not through glass or sunglasses.

schedule.what: Look at the day sky from a window, and say what you see.

activities.record: Tell a grown-up three things you saw in the sky.

setup.art: A girl and a grown-up at a window of a flat, looking at a blue sky with clouds and a flying crow, the Sun out of view above the window.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the day sky. What can you see?

setup.art: A girl pointing at the sky out of a window and telling a grown-up what she sees, with a thought bubble of a dark sky.
setup.caption: 2. Say what you see. Guess the night sky.

flow.do: Stand at a window or on the balcony with your child. Ask them to name everything they can see in the sky.
flow.say: Let's look at the sky. Don't look at the Sun. What can you see up there?
flow.kid: Look at the sky. Not at the Sun! What can you see?
flow.parent: Sometimes the Moon can be seen in the day sky, as a pale white shape. If you spot it, point it out.

flow.do: Ask what makes the day sky bright, and whether it is warm by the window.
flow.say: Why is the sky so bright now? Put your hand on the window glass. Is it warm?
flow.kid: Why is the sky bright? Touch the window. Is it warm?

flow.do: Ask your child what the night sky will show. Listen to the guesses.
flow.say: Tonight, what will we see in the sky? Will the Moon be there? Will there be stars?
flow.kid: What will the night sky show?

ask.q: What will the night sky show?

flow.parent: Don't give answers. The torch star test will help your child find out about the stars.

activities.title: Window Star Count: lights on, lights off
activities.context: In this activity you count the stars you can see from a window at night. Then you switch off the lights near you, wait, and count again.

materials.item: a window or a balcony with some open sky, on a clear night
paper and a pencil for tally marks

activities.safety: A grown-up stays with your child on the balcony at all times.

schedule.what: On a clear night, count the stars from a window with the lights on, then with them off.

activities.record: Make two rows of tally marks: stars seen with the lights on, and stars seen with the lights off.

setup.art: A girl and a grown-up at a balcony at night with a lit room behind them, counting three stars over the buildings.
setup.caption: 1. Count the stars with the room lights on.

setup.art: The same balcony with the room behind dark, the girl's eyes wide, and a few more stars showing in the sky.
setup.caption: 2. Switch the lights off. Wait. Count again.

flow.do: On a clear night, stand at the window or on the balcony with the room lights on. Your child counts the stars and makes a tally mark for each.
flow.say: Let's count the stars we can see. Make one mark for each star.
flow.kid: Count the stars. Make one mark for each star.

flow.do: 1. Switch off the room lights behind you, and any balcony light. 2. Wait about two minutes in the dark, so your eyes get used to it. 3. Count again.
flow.say: Now we switch off our lights and wait a little. Our eyes need time in the dark. Now count again.
flow.kid: Lights off. Wait. Now count the stars again.

ask.q: Did you see more stars this time?

flow.parent: Street lights will still light up the sky, so you may find only one or two more stars. That still shows the idea. If it is cloudy, try another night.

flow.do: Ask where the new stars came from.
flow.say: Did new stars come out when we switched off our lights? Or were they there all along?
flow.kid: Were the new stars there all along? Why do you think so?

good: Yes, our lights were hiding them.
They were there, but too faint to see.

activities.title: Who Loves the Sunshine? A window hunt
activities.context: In this activity you look for people, animals, plants and things at home that use the Sun's light and heat.

materials.item: nothing to buy: your home and a window, on a sunny morning

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun.

schedule.what: Look around the home and out of the window for who and what uses the sunshine.

activities.record: Draw three things you found that use sunshine, and colour the Sun's light falling on each.

setup.art: A potted tulsi plant on a sunny windowsill, with their leaves turned towards the window, and a boy pointing at it.
setup.caption: 1. Look for a plant near a window. Which way do their leaves face?

setup.art: Out of a window, a crow sitting in the morning sun on a ledge, and clothes drying on a balcony line next door.
setup.caption: 2. Look out of the window. Who is using the sunshine?

flow.do: Look at a potted plant near a window with your child.
flow.say: Look at this plant by the window. Which way are their leaves turned? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the plant's leaves. Which way do they face? Why?

ask.q: Why do the leaves face the window?
good: The plant needs light to make food.

flow.parent: A plant senses where the light is and turns their leaves towards it. They make their food from sunlight, air and water.

flow.do: Look out of the window together for anyone or anything using sunshine.
flow.say: Who is using the sunshine out there? Look for birds, animals, people and things.
flow.kid: Who is using the sunshine? Look for birds, people and things.

good: A crow sitting in the sun.
A dog lying in a sunny spot.

flow.parent: Look for birds sitting in the morning sun to warm up, clothes or papad drying, and solar panels on a roof.

flow.do: Ask what the sunshine gave each one.
flow.say: What did the sunshine give the plant? The crow? The clothes? Was it light, or heat, or both?
flow.kid: What did the sunshine give each one? Light, heat or both?

good: The clothes dry in the heat.

games.title: Day Sky or Night Sky? A card sorting game
games.players: 1 or more players, and a grown-up to read the cards. Players take turns.
games.context: This is a card game. You sort cards into the day sky, the night sky, or both.

items.b: DAY. When we can see the Sun, it is day where we are.
DAY. Sunlight lights up the air and makes the sky blue.
NIGHT, to see them. The stars are there all day too, but the bright sky hides them.
NIGHT. A full Moon rises as the Sun sets, and shines all night with sunlight.
BOTH. A half Moon can often be seen in the afternoon sky, and in the evening too.
DAY. The Sun's heat dries them.
NIGHT. Many owls hunt at night, with their big eyes and sharp ears.

items.f: A crow warming up on a ledge
items.b: DAY. Crows sit in the morning sun to get warm.
NIGHT. We switch on lights when the Sun's light is gone.

items.f: A shadow on the floor from the window
items.b: DAY. Sunlight through the window makes the shadow.
BOTH. Clouds float in the sky by day and by night.
NIGHT. Many bats fly out at dusk to find food.
NIGHT. Fireflies make their own light. We see it best in the dark.

rules: Mix the 13 cards and put them in a pile, face down.
Make three places on the floor: a yellow paper for DAY, a dark paper for NIGHT, and a place in the middle for BOTH.
Players take turns. On your turn, take the top card. A grown-up reads the front out.
Put it on DAY, NIGHT or BOTH, and say why.
A grown-up turns the card over and reads the back. If you were right, keep the card in front of you. If not, put it on the right place.
When all 13 cards are sorted, count the cards each player kept. The player with the most cards wins. With one child, try to beat your last count. Play again to keep more.
At the end, talk about the stars card: are the stars in the sky in the day?

setup.art: Thirteen cards in a pile on the floor, with a yellow paper, a dark blue paper, and a space in the middle between them.
setup.caption: 1. Put out a yellow paper, a dark paper and a space for both.

setup.art: A girl putting the card 'A pale half Moon' in the middle, and a grown-up turning over another card.
setup.caption: 2. Sort each card. Turn it over to check.

flow.do: Lay out the papers. Read the rules together.
flow.say: Yellow is for the day sky. Dark is for the night sky. The middle is for things we see in both.
flow.kid: Yellow is day. Dark is night. The middle is both.

flow.do: Play through all 13 cards. Read each front, wait for your child's choice and reason, then read the back.
flow.say: Many twinkling stars. Day, night or both? Why? Let's turn it over.
flow.kid: Read the card. Day, night or both? Why? Turn it over.
flow.parent: The stars and the Moon cards are the tricky ones. Remind your child of the torch star test if they have done it.

flow.do: Talk about the stars card.
flow.say: We put the stars on night. But are the stars in the sky right now, in the day?
flow.kid: Are the stars in the sky right now?

games.title: Sun Up, Sun Down: a moving game
games.players: 2 or more players. One person is the caller and reads the cards. The others do the moves.
games.context: This is a moving game. The caller reads a card, and everyone shows with their hands and body what happens in the sky.

items.b: Stand tall and stretch your arms wide. Light and heat are coming.
Crouch down low. It is getting dark.
Open and close your fingers fast, like twinkling stars.
Keep twinkling, but hide your hands behind your back. You still shine, but nobody can see you.
Make a big circle with your arms. Turn your face towards the paper Sun, because your light comes from the Sun.
Fan your face. Phew, it is warm.
Hold your hands over your head like a roof. Ahh, cooler.
Melt slowly down to the floor.

items.f: A crow in the morning sun!
items.b: Puff yourself up and flap once. Warm feathers!
Lean your whole body towards the window, like leaves turning to the light.

rules: Stick a yellow paper Sun on a wall at one end of the room. This is the Sun.
Mix the 10 caller cards. The caller holds them.
The caller reads the front of a card, and then the back. A grown-up reads for a caller who cannot read yet.
Everyone else does the move on the back of the card.
After all 10 cards, swap the caller, and play again.

setup.art: A yellow paper Sun stuck on a wall at one end of a room, and a boy holding up a card that says Sun up while a girl stretches her arms wide.
setup.caption: 1. Stick up a paper Sun. The caller reads a card.

setup.art: Two children twinkling their fingers behind their backs, as the caller holds a card that says Stars in the day.
setup.caption: 2. Everyone does the move.

flow.do: Practise 'Stars at night' and 'Stars in the day' together.
flow.say: Stars at night: twinkle your fingers. Stars in the day: keep twinkling, but hide your hands behind your back.
flow.kid: Stars at night: twinkle! Stars in the day: twinkle behind your back.

flow.do: Play all 10 cards. After 'Stars in the day', ask why the hands are hidden.
flow.say: Stars in the day! Are you still twinkling? Why can nobody see you?
flow.kid: Do each move. Why can nobody see the day stars?

ask.q: Why can nobody see the stars in the day?

flow.do: Finish with the Moon card and ask one question.
flow.say: When you were the Moon, which way did you face? Why?
flow.kid: When you were the Moon, which way did you face?

ask.q: Why did the Moon face the Sun?
good: The Moon's light comes from the Sun.
The Sun lights the Moon up.

projects.title: My Day Sky and Night Sky Book
projects.context: In this project you make a small book. One half shows the day sky, and the other half shows the night sky, from your own window.

materials.item: two sheets of paper, folded in half and stapled or tied with thread to make a small book
crayons, including yellow, blue and black or dark blue

projects.safety: Never look straight at the Sun. A grown-up stays with your child on the balcony at night.

schedule.what: In the day, make the book and draw the day sky pages.
After dark, look out of the same window and draw the night sky pages.

projects.record: The finished book, with the day sky on the first pages and the night sky on the last pages.

setup.art: Two sheets of paper folded and stapled into a small book, with a yellow Sun drawn on the cover.
setup.caption: 1. Make a small book from two folded papers.

setup.art: A girl at a window in the day, drawing a blue sky, clouds and birds in the book.
setup.caption: 2. In the day, draw the day sky.

setup.art: The same girl at the window at night with a grown-up, drawing the Moon and a few stars on a dark page.
setup.caption: 3. At night, draw the night sky from the same window.

flow.do: A grown-up folds the two papers in half, puts one inside the other, and staples or ties them at the fold. Your child draws a Sun and a Moon on the cover.
flow.say: We are making a sky book. The front pages are for the day sky, and the back pages are for the night sky.
flow.kid: Make your sky book. Draw a Sun and a Moon on the cover.

flow.do: In the day, your child looks out of the window and draws the day sky on the first two pages. Write their words under the pictures.
flow.say: Look out of the window. Draw what you see in the day sky. What is making it so bright?
flow.kid: Draw the day sky. What makes it so bright?

ask.q: What makes the day sky bright?

flow.do: After dark, look out of the same window. Switch off the room light. Your child draws the night sky on the last pages.
flow.say: It is the same window, at night. What can you see now? Can you see the Moon? How many stars?
flow.kid: Same window, at night. Draw the Moon and the stars.
flow.wait: Do this step after dark, on the same day or the next day.
flow.parent: If the Moon is not up, or it is cloudy, your child can draw what they see and try again another night.

flow.do: Look at the day pages and the night pages side by side.
flow.say: Look at your day pages and your night pages. Were the stars in the sky in the day too? Where does the Moon get its light?
flow.kid: Were the stars there in the day? Where does the Moon's light come from?

ask.q: Were the stars there in the day?
good: Yes, but the bright sky hid them.
Yes, like the torch star by the window.

ask.q: Where does the Moon's light come from?
good: The Sun shines on the Moon.

challenges.title: Save the Ice Cube from the Sunshine (if you have a sunny spot)
challenges.context: This is a problem to solve. An ice cube is sitting in the sunshine. How can you keep it from melting for as long as you can?
challenges.problem: Kamala, a girl in Class 1, must keep an ice cube in a patch of sunshine. She wants it to last as long as it can. What can she use to help it?
constraints: The ice cube must stay in the same sunny spot.
Use only things you already have at home.
You may not put it back in the fridge.
materials: two ice cubes of the same size
paper, a cloth napkin, a steel lid, a cardboard box, a plastic cup
general: People sit in the shade of a tree or an umbrella on hot days.
Shops put cloth or tin sheets over their fronts to make shade.
Many people keep water cool in a clay pot in the shade.
creative: Make a little roof for the ice from a piece of cardboard.
Cover the bowl with a folded cloth napkin.
Stand a box between the Sun and the ice, so the ice sits in its shade.
challenges.your_turn: Try one idea on one ice cube. Leave the other ice cube with nothing. Which melted slower? Why do you think your idea worked or did not work?

setup.art: Two steel bowls with ice cubes in a sun patch on the floor, and beside them paper, a cloth, a steel lid and a small box.
setup.caption: 1. Two ice cubes in the sunshine. What can protect one?

setup.art: One bowl under a little cardboard roof, in its own small shade, and the other bowl in full sunshine.
setup.caption: 2. Try your idea. Which ice lasts longer?

flow.do: Read the problem to your child and show the things they may use.
flow.say: An ice cube must stay in the sunshine. How can we help it last longer? What could we use?
flow.kid: How can you keep the ice from melting? What could you use?

good: Put a box in front of it.

flow.do: Your child sets up their idea on one ice cube, and leaves the other with nothing. Check both after 5 and 10 minutes.
flow.say: Put your idea on one ice cube. Leave the other one with nothing. Let's check them after five minutes.
flow.kid: Try your idea on one ice cube. Check both after five minutes.
flow.parent: Anything that makes shade will help, because it stops the sunshine from reaching the ice. A steel lid in full sun can get warm itself, which is a good thing to notice.

flow.do: Ask which ice lasted longer and why.
flow.say: Which ice cube lasted longer? Why did your idea help?
flow.kid: Which lasted longer? Why?

check.q: Kamala, a girl in Class 1, puts a cardboard roof over one ice cube in the sunshine. Why does that ice last longer?
options: The roof makes shade, so less sunshine reaches the ice
The roof makes the ice heavier
check.why: The roof blocks the sunshine. The ice sits in shade, so less of the Sun's heat reaches it.

items.p: A grown-up reads each one. Does the Sun give it light, heat or both? Draw a line to the right box.
items: A bright room in the day
A sunny patch on the floor
items.why: The Sun gives light and heat together. A sunny patch is bright and warm, so it is both. A strong answer sees that some things use mostly the light, like a leaf making food, and some use mostly the heat, like drying clothes.

items.p: Three of these are safe to do in the sun. Which one is not safe? Circle it.
opts: Feeling the sunshine on your hand
Drying clothes on a sunny line
Sitting in the shade of a tree
items.why: Looking straight at the Sun, even for a moment, can hurt your eyes. The other three are safe.

items.p: Meena has wet clothes. Where will they dry fastest?
items.why: The Sun's heat dries clothes. In the sunshine they get more heat, so the water goes into the air faster.

items.p: The Moon is a ball of rock that goes round the Earth.
items.why: True. The Moon is a big ball of rock. It makes no light of its own, and shines with the Sun's light.

items.p: Draw yourself on a hot day. Show where the sunshine falls and where the shade is. Colour the place you would sit to stay cool.
items.a: A drawing with sunshine on one side and shade on the other, and the child sitting in the shade.
items.why: A strong drawing shows shade where something blocks the sunlight, and sunshine where it does not.
items.art: An empty box with a tree, a wall and a sunny patch of ground, ready for the child to draw in.

items.p: Draw a line from each sky thing to where its light comes from.
items.why: The Sun and the stars make their own light. The Moon has none of its own: it shines with sunlight.
items.art: A Sun, a Moon and a star on the left. On the right, a small Sun with rays labelled 'light from the Sun' and a glowing dot labelled 'its own light'.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why was the torch star hard to see by the bright window?
items.a: The light all around it was so bright that the small star got lost. The torch was still shining.
items.why: A strong answer says the torch kept shining, and that the bright light around it hid the star.

items.p: Look at this picture of a night sky over a city. Count the stars. Write the number.
items.why: There are 4 stars. In a city, the lights hide most of the faint stars, so we see only a few bright ones.
items.art: A night sky over a row of lit buildings and street lights, with a half Moon and exactly 4 star dots.

items.p: It is a hot afternoon. A family is talking about the sunshine.

views.says: Sunshine is wonderful. It dries our clothes, warms the water and helps the plants grow.
Sunshine is too hot now. Stay in the shade, or you will get tired and thirsty.
I want to play in the sun. It is the brightest time of day.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one good thing about someone else's idea. Say it, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: Any choice with a good reason. Sunshine brings useful light and heat. Too much of its heat in the afternoon can be hard on bodies, so shade helps then.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason, and fairly says something good about another view. The Sun's heat helps us, and too much of it can be too hot.

items.p: Look at this room in the day. A grown-up points to each place. Say 'warm' or 'cool', and the grown-up writes it.
labels: the floor in the sun patch
items.why: Places where sunlight falls get warmer. Places in the shade get less of the Sun's heat, so they stay cooler.
items.art: A room with a bright sun patch on the floor from a window, a table with shade under it, a sunny windowsill and a shady corner, each with an empty label.

items.p: A solar water heater on a roof warms bath water. What does it use from the Sun?
items.why: Sunshine brings heat. The solar water heater catches the Sun's heat and uses it to warm the water.

items.p: Put these in order, 1 to 4: what happened in the torch star test? A grown-up reads each line.
items: We made a tiny hole in the cardboard over the torch.
By the bright window, the star was hard to see.
In the dark room, the star was bright.
We found that the torch was shining all the time.
items.why: First the star was made. It was hard to see in a bright place, and easy to see in the dark. So the torch had been shining all along.

items.p: A white cloud can look bright in the day because sunlight falls on it.
items.why: True. A cloud makes no light of its own. It looks bright and white because the Sun shines on it.

items.p: A friend says, 'The Sun is so far away that it cannot warm me.' What would you tell your friend? Use the ice test. Say it, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: The Sun's light travels all the way here, and it brings heat. In the ice test, nothing touched the ice except sunshine, but the ice in the sunshine melted first.
items.why: A strong answer uses the ice test as evidence: only sunshine reached the ice, and it melted first, so the sunshine brought heat.

items.p: Draw the Sun, the Moon and the Earth. Draw an arrow to show the Sun's light going to the Moon, and another arrow from the Moon to the Earth.
items.a: A Sun with an arrow to the Moon, and an arrow from the Moon to the Earth.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the light starting at the Sun, landing on the Moon, and bouncing on to the Earth.
items.art: An empty space with three small circles: a big one on the left, a small one in the middle and a middle-sized one on the right.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 1, counts 3 stars from her balcony with all the lights on. She switches off the lights and waits. What will she most likely see?
items.why: The lights near her made the sky around her a little brighter. With them off, some fainter stars can be seen. They were there all along.

items.p: Three of these happen because of the Sun's heat. Which one does not? Circle it.
opts: Ice melting on a sunny ledge
Wet clothes drying on a sunny balcony
A railing getting warm in the sunshine
items.why: The Moon shines with the Sun's light, not its heat. The other three happen because sunshine brings heat.

items.p: Look at this picture of the day sky. A grown-up points to each thing. Say 'makes its own light' or 'shines with the Sun's light', and the grown-up writes it.
items.why: Only the Sun makes its own light in this picture. The Moon and the cloud look bright because sunlight falls on them.
items.art: A blue day sky with the Sun at one edge, a pale half Moon and a white cloud, each with an empty label.

items.p: Why do children in a village far from a town see more stars than children in a big city? Say it, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: The city has many lights, which make the night air glow. That hides the faint stars. In the village the sky is darker, so more stars can be seen.
items.why: A strong answer says the stars are the same, and the lights around us change how many we can see.

items.p: Two friends are talking about the stars in the daytime.

views.says: The stars are still there in the day. We can't see them because the sky is so bright.
If we can't see the stars in the day, how do we know they are there? Maybe they really go away.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? What evidence would you show the other friend? Say it, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: Most children agree with Priya and show the torch star test, or tell Arjun about a total eclipse, when stars appear in the day. Arjun's question is still a good one: a scientist asks how we know.
items.why: A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence. It also says why Arjun's question is fair: we should ask how we know something we cannot see.

quiz.p: What two things does the Sun give us?
quiz.why: The Sun gives light and heat together. You can feel the heat in a patch of sunshine.

quiz.p: Which of these is a star?
quiz.why: The Sun is a star: a huge ball of hot gas that makes its own light. The Moon and clouds only look bright when sunlight falls on them.

quiz.p: Why does the Moon look bright at night?
quiz.why: The Moon is a ball of rock. It makes no light of its own. Sunlight falls on it and bounces down to us.

quiz.p: Where are the stars in the daytime?
opts: Still in the sky, hidden by the bright day sky
quiz.why: The stars shine all the time. The Sun makes the day sky so bright that their small light cannot be seen.

quiz.p: In the torch star test, what changed between the bright window and the dark room?
quiz.why: It was a fair test: the torch, the hole and the distance stayed the same. Only the light around the star changed.

opts: Feeling the Sun's warmth on your hand
Looking straight at the Sun for a moment
Looking at the Sun through sunglasses
quiz.why: Feeling the warmth is safe. Looking at the Sun, even for a moment or through sunglasses, can hurt your eyes.

quiz.p: Meera's ice cube is in a sunny spot. What will help it last longer?
opts: Putting a cardboard roof over it to make shade
Moving it closer to the window
Putting it on a black plate in the sun
quiz.why: Shade blocks the sunshine, so less of the Sun's heat reaches the ice.

quiz.p: Ravi puts one steel spoon in the sunshine and one in the shade for 10 minutes. Which spoon feels warmer?
quiz.why: Sunshine brings heat. The spoon in the sunshine gets more of it.

quiz.p: Why is the sky bright in the daytime?
opts: The stars shine more by day
quiz.why: Sunlight lights up the air and makes the whole day sky bright. That bright sky hides the stars.

quiz.p: A total eclipse of the Sun makes the sky dark in the middle of the day. What can people see then?
quiz.why: When the Moon covers the Sun, the sky goes dark, and bright stars appear. They were there all day.

videos.title: Stars appearing as the sky darkens, a time-lapse from dusk to night
videos.why: Shows the stars appearing one by one as the Sun's light fades, so a child sees they were there all along.
videos.check: Find a real time-lapse of a dusk sky turning to night, ideally filmed in India. Check it is real footage, not animation, and that the Sun is never shown straight on for long.

videos.title: A total eclipse of the Sun: the sky goes dark at midday
videos.why: Shows day turning dark for a few minutes, with bright stars or planets appearing, which is the real-sky version of the torch star test.
videos.check: Find real footage of a total solar eclipse, such as the one of 22 July 2009 seen across India, from a science agency or a news channel. Check it shows the sky darkening, and that it warns never to look at the Sun without proper eclipse glasses.

videos.title: Chandrayaan-3 landing on the Moon
videos.why: Shows the Moon as grey rock and dust up close, lit by sunlight, not a lamp.
videos.check: Find ISRO's own video of the Chandrayaan-3 landing on 23 August 2023 or the pictures from its lander. Check it is from ISRO or a trusted news channel, and pick a short part with clear pictures of the Moon's ground.

applications: Solar panels on roofs and at railway stations turn sunlight into electricity.
Families dry clothes, papad, vadam and chillies in the sunshine, because the Sun's heat dries them.
Solar water heaters on many flat roofs use the Sun's heat to warm bath water.
India's Aditya-L1, launched in 2023, is a spacecraft that watches the Sun all the time. Its project director was Nigar Shaji, a scientist from Tenkasi in Tamil Nadu.
Some cities and parks keep their lights low at night so that people, birds and insects can see the stars and the dark again.

spotted.text: At Pongal in Tamil Nadu, families cook sweet pongal outside in the morning sunshine, to thank the Sun for the harvest.
spotted.art: A clay pot of pongal boiling over on a small fire outside a house in the morning sun, with a kolam on the ground.

spotted.text: At Chhath Puja in Bihar, people stand in rivers and ponds at sunset and sunrise to greet the Sun.
spotted.art: Women standing in a river at sunrise holding baskets of fruit, with the Sun low on the water.

spotted.text: At the Sun Temple in Konark, Odisha, the temple is built like a giant chariot for the Sun, with huge stone wheels.
spotted.art: A big carved stone wheel on the wall of an old temple, with sunlight falling across it.

spotted.text: On Sharad Purnima, many families in Gujarat and Maharashtra sit out under the full Moon and share sweet milk.
spotted.art: A family on a terrace at night under a big full Moon, sharing bowls of sweet milk.

spotted.text: In the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, far from town lights, the night sky is full of stars.
spotted.art: A flat white salt desert at night under a sky crowded with stars.

spotted.text: On rooftops in Kerala and Karnataka, people spread coconut pieces and chillies on mats to dry in the sun.
spotted.art: A roof with mats of drying coconut pieces and red chillies in bright sunshine, with coconut trees around.

spotted.text: At Hanle in Ladakh, India has an observatory and a dark-sky reserve, where lights are kept low so the stars can be seen.
spotted.art: A white telescope dome on a bare brown hill at night, under a sky full of stars.

open_questions.why_open: Our galaxy alone has hundreds of billions of stars, and there are billions of galaxies. Nobody can count them all, and scientists' best guesses still differ.

open_questions.q: Is anyone living near another star, looking at our Sun?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found thousands of planets going round other stars. Nobody knows yet if any of them has life.

open_questions.q: Why does the Sun's outer glow get hotter than the Sun's surface?
open_questions.why_open: The Sun's faint outer glow, the corona, is much hotter than the bright surface below it. Scientists have ideas about why, and spacecraft like Aditya-L1 are studying it, but they do not know for sure yet.

ask_kids: Where is the sunniest spot in our home right now?
Is the Moon in the sky today? Let's look.
Where are the stars right now?
Which feels warmer, the balcony railing or the shady wall?
Why do we switch on lights when the Sun goes down?

jokes.j: Why did the star stay quiet all day?
jokes.a: Because the Sun was doing all the shining!

jokes.j: Why does the Moon never need a torch?
jokes.a: The Sun lends it light every night!

jokes.j: Why did the Sun not go to college?
jokes.a: The Sun already had millions of degrees!

jokes.j: What did the shade say to the sunshine?
How does the Moon get a haircut?
Why did the crow sit in the sun?
What is a star's favourite game?
Why did the Moon skip dinner?

maths.problem: Kavya, a girl in Class 1, counted 3 stars from her balcony with the lights on. With the lights off she counted 7. How many more stars did she see?
maths.explain: Count on from 3 to 7: 4, 5, 6, 7. That is 4. So she saw 4 more stars once the lights near her were off. Those stars were there all along.
maths.context: This is about the Window Star Count, where you counted stars with the lights on and off.
maths.why_maths: Taking one count away from the other shows how many stars the lights were hiding.

maths.problem: Divya, a girl in Class 1, did the ice test. She looked at both ice cubes every 5 minutes. The sunny one was gone at the 3rd look. The shady one was gone at the 6th look. Which lasted longer? How many more looks did it last?
maths.explain: 6 is more than 3, so the shady ice lasted longer. From 3 to 6 is 3 more looks. Each look was 5 minutes apart, so that is 15 more minutes in the shade.
maths.context: This is about the ice test, with one ice cube in the sunshine and one in the shade.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers shows how much longer the ice lasts when the Sun's heat cannot reach it.

maths.problem: Tara, the girl in the story, draws a sky pattern: Sun, Moon, star, Sun, Moon, star, Sun, Moon. What comes next?
maths.explain: The pattern is Sun, Moon, star, again and again. After Sun and Moon comes a star.
maths.context: This is about a sky pattern for a Day Sky and Night Sky Book.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern lets us say what comes next without looking.

maths.problem: Nila, a girl in Class 1, played the sorting game. She put 5 cards on DAY, 6 on NIGHT and 2 on BOTH. Which pile had the most cards? Nila says, 'So there are more things in the night sky than in the day sky.' Is she right?
maths.answer: NIGHT had the most. But the stars are in the day sky too, just hidden, so the night pile is only what we can see.
maths.explain: 6 is more than 5 and more than 3, so NIGHT had the most. But the stars card went on NIGHT only because we can see the stars at night. They are in the sky in the day too.
maths.context: This is about the Day Sky or Night Sky card game.
maths.why_maths: Counting each pile lets us compare them, and then we can ask what the numbers really tell us.

warmup.q: What two things does the Sun give us?
Does the Moon make its own light?
warmup.a: No. The Sun lights it up.

warmup.q: Where are the stars in the daytime?
warmup.a: Still in the sky. The bright day sky hides them.

warmup.q: Which ice cube melts first, in the sun or in the shade?

warmup.a: Yes, the nearest star to us.

warmup.q: Should you ever look straight at the Sun?
warmup.a: No, never. It can hurt your eyes.

roots.context: We have felt the Sun's heat, and found that a small light can shine without being seen. Now we ask what that tells us about the sky, about ourselves and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: By the sunny window, our torch star was hard to see. In the dark room, it shone brightly. The torch did not change, and the real stars do not change from day to night either. They shine all day, but we see them only when the sky around them is dark.
deep_truth.habit: We say the stars 'come out' at night, as if they switch on like street lights. The torch test shows that a star can stay the same while the light around it changes.
deep_truth.evidence: In the torch star test, the same star was faint by the bright window and bright in the dark room. In a total eclipse of the Sun, stars appear at midday.

three.who_am_i: You are someone who lives in sunshine. The warmth on your skin and the light in your eyes come from the Sun.
three.what_is_life: Almost all life on Earth runs on the Sun. Plants turn their leaves to the sunshine and make their food from it, and humans and other animals eat the plants.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is under a sky full of stars, all day and all night. Our Sun is one of them, the one close enough to warm us.

roots.thread: The Sun is one star among countless others. In the day, its light fills our sky so brightly that all the other stars are hidden. At night, our side of the Earth turns away from the Sun, and the other stars can be seen again. The same Sun lights the Moon, warms the ice, dries the chillies and feeds the plants. The Sun, the Moon and the stars are aware in their own way, like every part of the world.

teachings.source: Rig Veda 1.50.2 (a hymn to Surya, the Sun)
teachings.teaching: The stars slip away like thieves, together with their beams, before the all-seeing Sun.
teachings.link: The old hymn says what everyone sees: the stars vanish at sunrise. The torch test shows that they do not really go anywhere. The Sun's bright light hides them.

teachings.teaching: The face of truth is covered by a golden lid. Open it, so that I can see.
teachings.link: Something very bright can hide what is behind it. The golden light of the Sun covers the day sky, and the stars behind it cannot be seen.

science.text: The stars shine all the time. Sunlight lights up the air and makes the day sky bright and blue, and that hides the much fainter light of the stars.
The Sun is a star. The Moon makes no light of its own, and shines with sunlight.

other_view.view: They say the Sun, the Moon and the stars are not aware of anything. To them, the Sun is only very hot gas, and the Moon is only rock. They think awareness belongs to living beings with nerves or brains.

practice.title: One star, five breaths
practice.say: On a clear evening, stand at the window with your child and switch off the room light. Find one star together. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly, five times, looking at that star. Then say: this star was shining all day, while we could not see it. If no star shows, sit by a sunny window in the day instead. Close your eyes and feel the warm light on your eyelids.
practice.kid: Find one star. Breathe in and out slowly, five times. That star shone all day too.

ask: The stars were there all day, though nobody could see them. Is something real even when nobody sees it?
The Sun's light hides the other stars. Can something very bright stop us seeing something else?
roots.art: A child at a dark window, looking up at one bright star, with the faint outline of a Sun drawn on the other side of the Earth below.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many people thought the stars went away in the daytime, or only came out at night. But people who watched a total eclipse of the Sun saw something strange. For a few minutes, the Moon covered the whole Sun. The sky went dark in the middle of the day, and bright stars and planets appeared. They had been there all along. One person who travelled far to see an eclipse was Annie Maunder, an astronomer from Ireland. In January 1898 she came to India, to a village called Talni, where the eclipse could be seen. She carried a small camera, bought with a little money from her old college. When the Moon covered the Sun, she photographed the Sun's faint outer glow, which can be seen only in an eclipse. Her picture showed a streamer of glow longer than anyone had photographed before. For many years, her pictures were often printed with her husband's name instead of hers. Today big telescopes can find bright stars even in the daytime sky.
how_we_found_out.who: Annie Maunder, an astronomer from Ireland
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought the stars went away in the daytime. Total eclipses of the Sun showed that when the Sun's light is blocked, the stars can be seen at midday, so they are there all the time.

founder: ideas/by_topic/the-universe-sun-moon-stars-and-planets.md: the founder's notes on tracking the Sun and the circle dance for the Sun's daily path fed the Sun Up, Sun Down moving game. Her deeper grids (galaxies, the expansion of the universe) and her scientist cards (Khana, Williamina Fleming, Wang Zhenyi) belong to later levels.

Curriculum entry sci.sky.sun-moon-stars.L1 (The Sun gives light and heat; the Moon and stars at night). No board chapter is listed for this level. The Level 3 unit goes on to why the Sun is a star and the stars look small, the Moon's reflected light in a model, and pinhole Sun viewing, so this unit does not repeat those experiments. The Level 1 light sources unit already teaches that the Sun is a star and what a light source is.
science: The day sky is bright because air scatters sunlight (Rayleigh scattering), which hides the much fainter starlight. During totality in a total solar eclipse, bright stars and planets become visible.

Annie S. D. Maunder photographed the solar corona at the total eclipse of 22 January 1898 from Talni, India, with a small camera bought with a grant from Girton College, recording a coronal streamer much longer than any photographed before (MacTutor biography; Oxford Dictionary of National Biography).

Rig Veda 1.50.2, Griffith's translation: 'The constellations pass away, like thieves, together with their beams, before the all-beholding Sun.' Isha Upanishad 15: 'The face of truth is covered with a golden disc.'
Aditya-L1 was launched by ISRO on 2 September 2023; its project director was Nigar Shaji, from Tenkasi district in Tamil Nadu. Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023.

The Sun is about 150 million km from the Earth, and sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach us. The Hanle Dark Sky Reserve in Ladakh was set up in 2022 around the Indian Astronomical Observatory.
